query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre‐sintering mechanical activation of W particles to remove native oxide films combined with rapid, pressure‐assisted spark plasma sintering (SPS) of a Cu-infiltrated composite will produce a W–Cu material with fewer interfacial voids and improved thermal transport, while maintaining mechanical durability under irradiation, compared to conventional infiltration or standard SPS processes.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix that exhibit native surface oxide films and are prone to void formation and phase separation when processed by typical infiltration or conventional sintering methods.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled, high‐energy ball milling (mechanical activation) step on the W particles to clean and roughen the surfaces prior to a rapid SPS consolidation of a Cu–W powder mixture.
generation.conditions: Processing under pressures and rapid heating conditions during SPS (below Cu’s boiling point) following a defined duration of mechanical activation that is optimized to remove oxide films without inducing excessive amorphization; service conditions are those of fusion‐reactor joints exposed to irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial bonding between W and Cu due to increased surface contact area and removal of insulating oxide films, leading to a more uniform microstructure with minimized voids.
generation.mechanism: The mechanical activation step cleans and roughens the W particle surfaces, increasing their wettability by Cu. Subsequent rapid SPS promotes diffusion bonding without significant melt-related issues, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation and yielding a composite with better thermal contact and mechanical strength under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The activated and SPS‐processed W–Cu composite will exhibit lower interfacial void density, improved thermal conductivity, and retained mechanical integrity under simulated irradiation compared to composites produced by direct molten Cu infiltration or standard SPS without pre‐activation.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods such as direct melt infiltration of Cu into a W skeleton and standard SPS of the mixture without prior mechanical activation.
generation.boundary: Processing temperatures must remain below the boiling point of Cu and the intervention is limited to the pre‐sintering stage. Service conditions are restricted to those relevant for fusion-reactor joint environments with irradiation exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal combination of milling time, energy input, and SPS parameters has not been fully determined; residual stresses or irradiation-induced changes at the interface might still affect long-term durability.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: (1) using the proposed mechanical activation followed by SPS and (2) a control group produced by conventional SPS without pre‐activation. Characterize both sets for interfacial microstructure and thermal/mechanical properties before and after exposure to simulated fusion reactor irradiation.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of interfacial void density using high-resolution microscopy
Mechanical tests (e.g., hardness, tensile strength) pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically activated/SPS composite does not exhibit significantly reduced void density, improved thermal conductivity, and superior mechanical performance under irradiation compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Casting [] and powder metallurgy [] are two common methods for preparing HEAs. For casting, there are two kinds of defects which are the vaporization of low melting-point elements and the elements segregation in the ingot []. For powder metallurgy, the HEAs can be prepared by MA and then consolidated. The HEAs powders prepared by MA are uniform and fine, and even form nanocrystalline. Hence a rapid sintering is needed to maintain this microstructure []. SPS is a new field-assisted sintering technique which can effectively suppress the grain coarsening by rapid heating and efficient densification in a few minutes [,,]. Compared with MA, gas atomization can produce more homogeneous powders. The preparation of HEAs powders by gas atomization is a rapid solidification process [], in which grain growth and element segregation are inhibited, and the high cooling rate even leads to the formation of an amorphous phase []. In the previous studies, two classical HEAs, CoCrFeNiMn with a single FCC phase and AlCoCrFeNi with a single BCC phase, have been extensively studied. One way to enhance the reactivity of the powder mixture is to activate it by treatment in various apparatuses, mainly planetary mills []. The main difference from the above-mentioned mechanical alloying approach is that mechanical activation (MA) does not last as long and does not lead to the formation of new phases. During MA, the powders are crushed and the surfaces of the particles are cleaned from the oxide films. The contact area between components increases. Often, it allows the decreasing of the initiation temperature and promotes a more complete reaction in mixtures that burn weakly without activation []. Since Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni refers to systems in which SHS is difficult or impossible (depending on the composition), MA can be used to initiate a reaction in them without the use of a thermally coupled reaction. Moreover, preliminary activated powders can be used not only for combustion synthesis, but also for reaction sintering, which is based on the idea of simultaneous synthesis and compaction of the material.
